2 ἐνώπιον cod. 3 παιδίον: cf. Dyroff, Sphaera, p. 536, ad vers. 7. 11 Haec femina
in sphaera Indorum collocata sine dubio Andromeda Graecorum est. 14 τὸ στήθη
et infra τὸ σκέλη cod. 17 σκορπίου in cod. sign. astronomico scriptum : cf. de
hac constellatione Sphaera, p. 257 et 539. τὰ βʹ ἥμισυ τὸ cod. 19 κοντιάριον
(sic cod.) ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ αὐτοῦ: haec iam in codd. Arab. corrupta sunt; “ neque voca-
bulum “ rumḥaṇ „ (lanceam) mutari potest, cum verbum “ rakaza „ de lancea
dicatur „ (Dyroff). Varahamihira habet “ with serpents entwined round his body „
ex versione Colebrookii; Achmes, cuius translatio non de Apomasare pendet (v.
Sphaera, p. 485), recte : τανύσας εἰς τὸν πόδα αὐτοῦ ὄφιν. 23-24 γυναικὸς τῆς
ζητούσης τὸν ἄνδρα i. e. Ἀνδρομέδα, cf. Sphaera, p. 429 not. et 489, 14.
sections.en: 2 ἐνώπιον ('before') the codex has. 3 παιδίον ('child'): cf. Dyroff, Sphaera, p. 536, ad vers. 7. 11 This woman placed in the sphere of the Indians is without doubt the Andromeda of the Greeks. 14 τὸ στήθη ('the breasts') and below τὸ σκέλη ('the legs') the codex has. 17 σκορπίου ('of the scorpion') written in the codex with an astronomical sign: cf. concerning this constellation Sphaera, p. 257 and 539. τὰ βʹ ἥμισυ τὸ ('the two and a half the') the codex has. 19 κοντιάριον ('spearman') (thus the codex) ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ αὐτοῦ ('in his belly'): these things are already corrupt in the Arabic codices; "neither can the word 'rumḥaṇ' (lance) be changed, since the word 'rakaza' is said of a lance" (Dyroff). Varahamihira has "with serpents entwined round his body" from the version of Colebrooke; Achmes, whose translation does not depend on Apomasar (see Sphaera, p. 485), correctly: τανύσας εἰς τὸν πόδα αὐτοῦ ὄφιν ('stretching a snake to his foot'). 23-24 γυναικὸς τῆς ζητούσης τὸν ἄνδρα ('of the woman seeking the man') i.e. Andromeda, cf. Sphaera, p. 429 not. and 489, 14.

summary.headline: Pisces Decans and Sinotic Signs
summary.text: Indian and Ptolemaic descriptions of the second and third decans of Pisces, including human figures, animals, and stellar constellations; the text then begins a discussion of the sinotic signs of the eyes and their degrees, naming the Pleiades, zodiacal signs, and related stars.
